FARL: An Applied Guide for Unidimensional Assessments

Source: vignettes/FARL.Rmd
FARL.Rmd

Overview

The FARL package fits factor-augmented regularized latent regression models for unidimensional assessments. It is designed for applications with many correlated background variables. The common variation in those variables is summarized by factor scores, while regularization identifies additional covariates that are useful for predicting the latent trait.

The applied workflow has two main steps:

  1. fit the population model with Farlr_mml(); and
  2. generate plausible values with Farlr_drawPVs().

Two estimation methods are available.

Method When to use it
FARLR_EMM Use when the goal is a sparse model estimated through the iterative regularized procedure.
FARLR_Debias Use when the goal is variable selection followed by a correction of regularization shrinkage. This is a useful default for reporting coefficient estimates.

The examples below focus on data preparation, function calls, output interpretation, and plausible-value analysis rather than algorithmic details.

Load FARL 

library(FARL)

Prepare the data

Farlr_mml() uses three required data objects.

Object Required organization Purpose
X Respondents by covariates Background variables used in the population model. All columns must be numeric, finite, and have nonzero variance.
Y Respondents by items Item responses. Rows must correspond exactly to the rows of X. Missing responses may be coded NA.
parTab One row per item Fixed item parameters. Its row order must match the column order of Y.

The package supports binary 1PL, 2PL, and 3PL items, as well as three-category GPCM items. Binary responses must be coded 0/1, and GPCM responses must be coded 0/1/2. The package determines item type from the supplied item parameters.

Example data

sim_a1 contains 300 respondents, 100 background variables, and six binary 2PL items. The true latent trait is retained only for simulation diagnostics.

data(sim_a1)

dim(sim_a1$X)
# [1] 300 100

dim(sim_a1$Y)
# [1] 300   6

head(sim_a1$Y)
head(sim_a1$X[, 1:6])
sim_a1$parTab

Before fitting the model, verify row alignment, item alignment, response codes, and missingness.

stopifnot(nrow(sim_a1$X) == nrow(sim_a1$Y))
stopifnot(nrow(sim_a1$parTab) == ncol(sim_a1$Y))

mean(is.na(sim_a1$Y))
table(sim_a1$Y, useNA = "ifany")

apply(sim_a1$X, 2, sd) |>
  summary()

Choose primary covariates

The main argument identifies covariates that must remain in the population model. These variables are not removed by penalized selection. Supply their column indices in X.

main <- c(1, 2, 15, 29, 45)

main_names <- if (is.null(colnames(sim_a1$X))) {
  paste0("X", main)
} else {
  colnames(sim_a1$X)[main]
}

main_names

Use main = integer(0) when every original covariate may be selected or excluded by regularization.

Fit FARL

Main fitting arguments

Argument Applied meaning
X, Y, parTab Data objects described above.
method Selects "FARLR_EMM" or "FARLR_Debias".
main Column indices of primary covariates that remain in the model.
lambda Candidate regularization values. A wider grid is useful when the selected value falls at an endpoint.
n_sam Monte Carlo sample size used during fitting. Larger values reduce simulation noise but increase runtime.
n_sam_final Monte Carlo sample size used in the final evaluation or debiased update.
K_hat Optional number of common factors. When omitted, FARL estimates it using parallel analysis.
delta.criteria Convergence tolerance for iterative updates.
iter.max Maximum number of iterations for each candidate regularization value.
window.size Number of recent updates used for stabilization.
proposal_inflation Controls the spread of the latent-trait proposal distribution used during Monte Carlo integration.
seed Makes factor selection and Monte Carlo calculations reproducible.
progress, verbose Control progress bars and printed fitting information.

The defaults provide a convenient starting point. For a final analysis, inspect convergence and check whether results remain stable with larger Monte Carlo sample sizes and a broader lambda grid.

Fit FARLR-Debias 

fit_debias <- with(
  sim_a1,
  Farlr_mml(
    X = X,
    Y = Y,
    parTab = parTab,
    method = "FARLR_Debias",
    main = main,
    lambda = seq(0.05, 0.50, length.out = 10),
    n_sam = 25L,
    n_sam_final = 60L,
    seed = 2026,
    progress = TRUE
  )
)

Fit FARLR-EMM

The input interface is the same; only method changes.

fit_emm <- with(
  sim_a1,
  Farlr_mml(
    X = X,
    Y = Y,
    parTab = parTab,
    method = "FARLR_EMM",
    main = main,
    lambda = seq(0.05, 0.50, length.out = 10),
    n_sam = 25L,
    n_sam_final = 60L,
    seed = 2026,
    progress = TRUE
  )
)

Examine a fitted FARL model

The fitted object contains the coefficient estimates together with the factor-adjusted design, item information, scaling values, and fitting diagnostics needed for later plausible-value generation.

Component Interpretation
coefficients Named regression coefficients. Names beginning with FS refer to common-factor scores; names beginning with X refer to original covariates.
sigma Residual standard deviation of the latent trait after conditioning on the fitted predictors.
lambda Selected regularization value.
LogLik Objective or likelihood summary returned for the selected model.
Convergence Method-specific convergence indicator.
factor_scores Estimated common-factor scores for each respondent.
K_hat Number of common factors used in the fitted model.
hatU Factor-adjusted covariates used by FARLR_Debias.
Fan Final factor-plus-adjusted-covariate design used by FARLR_Debias.
X, X_center, X_scale Standardized covariates and the values used to standardize them.
item_params, item_type Item parameters and detected response-model type.
stuDat, stuItems Subject-level design information and long-format item responses retained for compatibility and PV generation.

Check method and convergence 

fit_debias$method
fit_debias$K_hat
fit_debias$lambda
fit_debias$LogLik
fit_debias$Convergence

names(fit_debias)

If the selected lambda is the smallest or largest candidate, extend the grid and refit. If the model does not converge, increase iter.max, review the input variables, and assess stability across seeds and Monte Carlo settings.

Summarize coefficients

Printing every coefficient is difficult when X is wide. A compact table of the largest coefficients is usually more informative.

coefficient_table <- data.frame(
  predictor = names(fit_debias$coefficients),
  coefficient = as.numeric(fit_debias$coefficients),
  row.names = NULL
)

coefficient_table$source <- ifelse(
  grepl("^FS", coefficient_table$predictor),
  "Common factor",
  "Original covariate"
)

coefficient_table <- coefficient_table[
  order(abs(coefficient_table$coefficient), decreasing = TRUE),
]

head(coefficient_table, 15L)

A positive coefficient indicates that higher values of the predictor are associated with a higher population mean for the latent trait, holding the other included predictors constant. Coefficients describe associations and should not be interpreted causally.

To inspect variables retained by the fitted model, apply a small numerical tolerance rather than comparing floating-point values directly with zero.

selection_tolerance <- 1e-8

selected_coefficients <- subset(
  coefficient_table,
  abs(coefficient) > selection_tolerance
)

selected_coefficients

The common-factor scores summarize shared variation across X. Covariate coefficients represent information that remains useful after the factor adjustment. Primary variables supplied through main should be interpreted alongside the selected covariates rather than as a separate model.

Interpret residual variation 

fit_debias$sigma
fit_emm$sigma

sigma is a residual standard deviation, not a variance. A smaller value indicates that the fitted population model leaves less latent-trait variation unexplained. Comparisons are most useful when the same data, item parameters, and latent scale are used.

Inspect the factor-adjusted design 

dim(fit_debias$factor_scores)
head(fit_debias$factor_scores)

dim(fit_debias$hatU)
dim(fit_debias$Fan)
head(colnames(fit_debias$Fan))

fit_debias$X_center[1:6]
fit_debias$X_scale[1:6]

FARLR_Debias uses Fan, which combines common-factor scores and factor-adjusted covariates. These stored objects are especially important when applying the model to new data or diagnosing unexpected coefficients.

Compare the two estimation methods 

method_comparison <- data.frame(
  method = c(fit_emm$method, fit_debias$method),
  lambda = c(fit_emm$lambda, fit_debias$lambda),
  sigma = c(fit_emm$sigma, fit_debias$sigma),
  nonzero_coefficients = c(
    sum(abs(fit_emm$coefficients) > selection_tolerance),
    sum(abs(fit_debias$coefficients) > selection_tolerance)
  ),
  row.names = NULL
)

method_comparison

Different coefficient counts are expected because the two methods perform estimation and shrinkage correction differently. Method choice should be made before inspecting the final results and should be checked through sensitivity analyses when substantive conclusions depend on a small set of variables.

Generate plausible values

Farlr_drawPVs() combines the fitted population model with each respondent’s observed item responses. It returns plausible values together with posterior summaries that are useful for checking the generated draws. Plausible values are intended for population and subgroup analyses, not for reporting an individual’s single score.

Plausible-value arguments

Argument Applied meaning
mmlcomp Object returned by Farlr_mml().
npv Number of plausible values generated for each respondent.
n_quad Number of points used to approximate each respondent’s posterior distribution.
theta_range Lower and upper limits of the initial latent-score grid.
adaptive_range When TRUE, allows the grid to expand for respondents whose fitted prior lies near or beyond the initial limits.
range_sd Controls how far the adaptive grid extends around the fitted prior mean.
design_matrix Optional replacement design matrix. Normally omitted so that FARL reconstructs the fitted design automatically.
theta Optional true trait values used only for simulation diagnostics. Omit this argument for real data.
seed Makes plausible-value generation reproducible.
return_details When TRUE, returns the PV matrix and posterior summaries in a list.

Draw plausible values 

farl_pvs <- Farlr_drawPVs(
  mmlcomp = fit_debias,
  npv = 10L,
  n_quad = 30L,
  theta_range = c(-4, 4),
  adaptive_range = TRUE,
  range_sd = 4,
  seed = 2026,
  progress = TRUE,
  return_details = TRUE
)

For simulation studies, theta = sim_a1$theta may be added to report the difference between the average posterior estimate and the average true trait. It should not be supplied in an empirical analysis.

Examine plausible-value output

Component Interpretation
data Numeric matrix containing only the plausible values.
datPVs Data frame containing respondent IDs and columns _farl1, _farl2, and so on.
EAP_estimates Respondent-level posterior means.
EAP_variance Respondent-level posterior variances.
posterior_mode Most likely grid value for each respondent.
prior_mean Latent-regression mean predicted by the fitted population model.
sigma Residual standard deviation copied from the fitted model.
mean_difference Simulation-only mean recovery diagnostic; NA when theta is omitted. 
names(farl_pvs)
dim(farl_pvs$data)

head(farl_pvs$datPVs)
summary(farl_pvs$EAP_estimates)
summary(farl_pvs$EAP_variance)

cor(farl_pvs$EAP_estimates, farl_pvs$prior_mean)

Large posterior variances identify respondents whose response patterns provide less information about the latent trait. Differences between prior_mean and EAP_estimates show how the observed item responses update predictions from the background variables.

Use plausible values in secondary analyses

Run the intended analysis separately for every plausible-value column and then combine the resulting estimates and uncertainty. Do not average the plausible values first and analyze that single average as if it were an observed score.

The following helpers summarize the overall spread across a set of plausible values. variance.sample() averages the respondent-level variance across PV datasets, while variance.cal() also accounts for variation among the PV dataset means.

variance.sample <- function(theta_matrix) {
  theta_matrix <- as.matrix(theta_matrix)
  mean(apply(theta_matrix, 2L, stats::var))
}

variance.cal <- function(theta_matrix) {
  theta_matrix <- as.matrix(theta_matrix)
  number_of_pvs <- ncol(theta_matrix)
  within_variance <- variance.sample(theta_matrix)
  between_variance <- stats::var(colMeans(theta_matrix))

  within_variance +
    (1 + 1 / number_of_pvs) * between_variance
}

pv_matrix <- farl_pvs$data

variance.sample(pv_matrix)
variance.cal(pv_matrix)

For a substantive regression, repeat the model for each plausible value and store the coefficient and its sampling variance.

analysis_data <- data.frame(
  outcome = sim_a1$X[, 1],
  group = sim_a1$X[, 2]
)

pv_results <- lapply(
  seq_len(ncol(farl_pvs$data)),
  function(pv_index) {
    model_data <- transform(
      analysis_data,
      plausible_value = farl_pvs$data[, pv_index]
    )

    model <- lm(plausible_value ~ group, data = model_data)

    data.frame(
      pv = pv_index,
      estimate = coef(model)["group"],
      sampling_variance = vcov(model)["group", "group"],
      row.names = NULL
    )
  }
)

pv_results <- do.call(rbind, pv_results)
pv_results

These stored estimates can then be combined using the multiple-imputation pooling procedure appropriate for the target analysis.

Mixed 3PL and GPCM responses

The same FARL workflow applies when the assessment contains both binary 3PL items and three-category GPCM items. sim_a2 demonstrates this case.

data(sim_a2)

dim(sim_a2$X)
dim(sim_a2$Y)
table(sim_a2$itemtype)

sim_a2$parTab[, c(
  "ItemID", "itemtype", "a", "b", "c", "b1", "b2"
)]

Fit the model and generate PVs using the same public functions.

fit_mixed <- with(
  sim_a2,
  Farlr_mml(
    X = X,
    Y = Y,
    parTab = parTab,
    method = "FARLR_Debias",
    main = main,
    seed = 2026
  )
)

table(fit_mixed$item_type)

pvs_mixed <- Farlr_drawPVs(
  mmlcomp = fit_mixed,
  npv = 10L,
  adaptive_range = TRUE,
  seed = 2026
)

head(pvs_mixed$datPVs)

For mixed-format assessments, check that every parTab row contains the parameters required by its item type. Missing responses remain coded as NA and are ignored for the corresponding item during posterior calculation.

Practical checks

Before reporting a FARL analysis, verify the following:

  • rows of X and Y refer to the same respondents;
  • rows of parTab match the item-column order in Y;
  • covariates are numeric and have nonzero variance;
  • response codes agree with their item types;
  • primary covariates in main are the intended columns of X;
  • the selected lambda is not constrained by an inadequate grid;
  • fitting results are stable across Monte Carlo seeds and larger sample sizes;
  • sigma is positive and convergence diagnostics are acceptable; and
  • all plausible values, rather than their respondent-level average, are used in secondary analyses.

Main FARL outputs

Function Main output
Farlr_mml() Coefficients, residual SD, selected regularization value, factor scores, factor-adjusted designs, item information, and fitting diagnostics.
Farlr_drawPVs() Plausible-value matrix, ID-based PV data frame, EAP estimates, posterior variances, posterior modes, and fitted prior means.
